title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 7
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Restaurant Reservation Issue
listeningScripts.text: Diner: Hi, I made a reservation for tonight at 7 PM under the name Anderson, and I just realized the name is spelled wrong in your system. Manager: Oh no, I'm sorry about that. Let me look that up. How is it spelled? Diner: A-N-D-E-R-S-O-N. I don't know how it got misspelled. Manager: I see it here as A-N-D-E-R-S-E-N. That's an easy mix-up. When you arrive, just let the host know and we'll get you seated right away. Diner: Actually, I'm calling because I need to change the time. Can I do 7:30 instead? Manager: Absolutely. Let me adjust that for you. How many people? Diner: Six of us. Manager: Perfect. I've moved you from 7 PM to 7:30 PM for six people, and I've corrected the name spelling. Is there anything else? Diner: Yes, one more thing. Can you make sure we have a quiet table? There are some business matters we want to discuss. Manager: I'll add a note to your reservation requesting a quieter area away from the bar. We have some nice tables by the window. Diner: That sounds great. What's your cancellation policy? Manager: We require 24 hours notice for cancellations. If you need to cancel, just call us before 7:30 PM tomorrow. Diner: Got it. Thank you.

listeningScripts.title: Apartment Viewing Discussion
listeningScripts.text: Renter: I'm interested in this one-bedroom apartment. What are the lease terms? Landlord: It's a one-year lease. The rent is $1,200 per month, due on the first of each month. Renter: That seems reasonable. What utilities are included? Landlord: Water and heating are included, but you pay for electricity and internet. Renter: I see. What about parking? Landlord: There's one dedicated parking spot in the lot. It's included in the rent. Renter: Perfect. When would I be able to move in? Landlord: If we sign the lease today, you can move in on July 1st. Renter: Is that two weeks from now? Landlord: Yes, exactly two weeks. Do you have any pets? Renter: I have a cat. Is that okay? Landlord: Yes, cats are allowed. There's a one-time pet deposit of $150. Renter: Alright. Can I get a few days to think about it? Landlord: Sure, take until the end of the week. After that, I have other interested renters.

listeningScripts.title: City Library Card Registration
listeningScripts.text: Hello, and welcome to the City Library system. I'm here to explain our library card registration process. A library card gives you access to millions of digital and physical resources. Registration is free and open to all residents with proof of address. Bring a government-issued ID and a recent utility bill or lease agreement. Visit any of our twelve branch locations during regular hours, Monday through Saturday, 9 AM to 6 PM, and Sunday 1 to 5 PM. Our main branch is downtown on Oak Street. Registration takes about ten minutes. Once registered, you can immediately borrow books, DVDs, and audiobooks. You're allowed up to twenty items at a time. Loan periods are three weeks for books, one week for DVDs, and four weeks for audiobooks. Late fees are twenty-five cents per day for books. Digital resources such as e-books and e-magazines are also available. Access them through our website anytime. Many online databases offer academic journals and local news archives. Children under eighteen need parental consent on their registration form. We also offer free Wi-Fi and computer access at all branches. Printing is available at ten cents per page. For questions, visit the information desk or call our hotline at 416-555-0198.

listeningScripts.title: Ontario Solar Energy Initiative
listeningScripts.text: Ontario has launched an ambitious solar energy initiative targeting rooftop installations across residential and commercial properties. The program, called SolarON, aims to install solar panels on 50,000 homes and businesses over three years. The government is providing subsidies covering up to 40 percent of installation costs for eligible homeowners. Solar power currently accounts for only 1.2 percent of Ontario's electricity generation, but officials project this could increase to 8 percent by 2030. The initiative includes training programs to develop 2,500 new solar installation technicians. A rebate program offers homeowners up to 8,000 dollars toward equipment and installation expenses. Companies installing solar systems have reported a 150 percent increase in inquiries since the program's announcement. Environmental advocates praise the initiative for reducing carbon emissions and creating green jobs. The average residential system costs approximately 22,000 dollars before subsidies and rebates. Participants are also eligible for net metering, allowing them to sell excess power back to the grid.

listeningScripts.title: Corporate Training Program Redesign
listeningScripts.text:
Human Resources Director Michelle: We're considering a complete redesign of our corporate training program. Our current approach is one-size-fits-all classroom training, and it's not effective. We want to move toward personalized learning paths and micro-credentials. The investment would be about 3.5 million dollars over three years, but studies show this approach increases employee retention by up to 35 percent.

Department Manager Kevin: I'm supportive of better training, but I'm skeptical about the cost and timeline. We're already stretched thin with current projects. Three years seems like a long time to see results. How quickly can we expect to see improvements in employee performance and retention?

Employee Development Specialist Nina: Kevin, the timeline actually makes sense. Year one is for system setup and rolling out the first pilot programs. By year two, we'll have meaningful data. We've seen in comparable companies that employee engagement scores improve within six months of launching personalized learning. Retention improvements typically follow within 12 to 18 months as employees feel more invested in their development.

CEO David: This aligns with our strategic goals. We're losing skilled employees to competitors, and part of the issue is they don't see clear development paths. If this program helps us retain talent and develop leadership from within, the 3.5 million investment is justified. But we need to ensure accountability. Nina, can you outline measurable metrics we'll track?

listeningScripts.title: Universal Basic Income Feasibility
listeningScripts.text: I want to discuss Universal Basic Income, or UBI, and why I believe it could work in Canada. The concept is straightforward: every citizen receives a regular, unconditional cash payment from the government. Now, I know people immediately worry about the cost, but let me address that. First, UBI could replace many existing welfare programs that are expensive to administer. The bureaucracy involved in means-testing and eligibility verification costs billions. UBI would be simpler and less wasteful. Second, the economic stimulus of putting money in people's hands is significant. When people have financial security, they spend more, which supports businesses and creates jobs. Third, UBI addresses real problems: poverty, economic instability, and lack of opportunity. We've seen pilot projects in Kenya, Finland, and Canada that show positive outcomes. In Kenya, UBI increased business formation by 32 percent. In Finland, participants reported better mental health and less anxiety. Some worry it will make people lazy, but that's not supported by evidence. People want purpose and contribution, not just money. What UBI does is give them the freedom to pursue education, care for family, or start businesses without desperation. The real question isn't whether we can afford UBI—it's whether we can afford not to implement it. Rising inequality and automation are creating unprecedented challenges.
